newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro stocks close at records, Wall St slips.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro stocks close at records, Wall St slips.

text.p: Leading European share markets finished at record closing levels on Tuesday despite slipping from new trading highs earlier in the day after Wall Street, their inspiration, turned lower.
On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar held steady as Japanese officials managed to halt a slide they provoked last week, while sterling firmed on signs that British interest rates would rise.
Stock markets all hit their highs -- in London and Germany record highs -- in the morning as investors reacted to Monday's 1.72 percent surge on Wall Street.
But the Europeans were often reluctant buyers as some analysts and traders said the markets were overbought and a correction was likely sooner or later.

In London, the FTSE 100 climbed for the 11th consecutive session to an early intraday record of 4,720.3 points. This was in reaction to Wall Street's surge overnight when investors gambled that the U.S. Federal Reserve would not put up interest rates when it holds a policy meeting on May 20.

But the London market turned after the Bank of England, newly empowered by the Labour government to decide interest rates, said that a further moderate tightening of British monetary policy would be needed.

Wall Street rose again briefly after the opening on Tuesday following relatively weak April retail sales. But by the time European markets closed the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 22.25 points (0.31 percent) at 7,270.50 due to profit taking.
This dragged the FTSE down almost 30 points from the record high to close at 4,691.0, still 21.4 points or 0.46 percent up on the day.
Faced with such a rapid rise in the past 10 days, London traders believe the euphoria will not last.
"This market is overbought and needs to come down. All it will take is a big one-day drop on Wall Street to set things in motion," one trader said.
But other traders said Wall Street still had some mileage in it after the retail sales figures, which showed a 0.3 percent drop as expected.
"The figures were smack in line and that's being viewed as a bullish sign," one dealer said.
"There is still a lot of money pouring into the U.S. market. People aren't expecting any aggressive Fed rate hikes so bond yields are dropping," another said.

But the market was still awaiting U.S. producer and consumer inflation data, due later this week, for a stronger indication of whether the Fed would move to tighten credit further on May 20, dealers said.

Paris was the strongest of the leading markets in percentage terms with the CAC 40 index of blue chips gaining about 1.4 percent in the morning. But it likewise fell from the highs and closed up 26.49 points or 0.98 percent at 2,719.58.
On the German markets the DAX index also climbed to an intraday record but it likewise slipped later.

"If there were major investor interest in the market the trading volumes would surely have to be higher than what we see right now," said one Frankfurt trader. "We've been at some lofty levels lately and it was time for some profit-taking."

The DAX index closed up 19.78 points (0.55 percent) at a record 3,595.15 before Wall Street opened. But in later post-bourse electronic dealings, the IBIS index was down 33.85 points (0.94 percent) at 3,559.29.

Deutsche Telekom closed floor trade down 1.06 marks at 40.13 marks on profit taking after the company announced a group net profit of 1.8 billion marks, a figure which analysts said was better than expected.

The dollar wobbled slightly after the soft U.S. retail sales data further deflated expectations of a near-term Federal Reserve interest rate rise, but earlier comments from Japanese finance and central bank officials created a steadier mood.

"It seems the Japanese have started to put the brakes on. Though they'e quite happy with current levels, they don't want to see (the dollar) steaming to 110 yen and below," said Pat Magill, head of the corporate desk at Daiwa Europe in London.
The dollar was at 118.95 yen in late trading after dipping to its lowest level in almost four months on Monday at 117.50.

"This has been such a choppy, rumour-driven market in recent days that the market seems to have stalled itself until a more concrete fix on events feeds through," said Julian Jessop, international economist at Nikko Europe.
Against the mark, the dollar was little changed from Monday just below the psychological 1.70 level at 1.6965 compared with 1.7035 late on Monday.
Sterling leapt over one pfennig after the Bank of England comments on monetary tightening in its quarterly inflation report. Later it retreated to around 2.7690 marks.
STOCK PRICES AT CLOSE
London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,691.0, up 21.4 points or 0.46 percent.
The Paris CAC-40 index closed up 26.49 points or 0.98 percent at 2,719.58.
The German DAX index closed up 19.78 points (0.55 percent) at a record 3,595.15. In later post-bourse electronic dealings, the IBIS index was down 33.85 points (0.94 percent) at 3,559.29.
CURRENCIES AT EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar stood at 1.6965 marks compared with 1.7035 late in Europe on Monday and 118.95 yen versus 118.86.
PRECIOUS METALS AT EUROPEAN CLOSE
Gold was at $348.35 an ounce closing at $348.75 in London on Monday. Silver was down three cents at $4.85. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
